questions.question: If these biases make us too quick to see consciousness in machines, could the same biases also make us miss real consciousness where it exists?

passages.quote: we become more likely to see consciousness where it doesn’t exist, and to miss seeing it where it does

questions.question: Doesn't the thought experiment of swapping brain parts for silicon ones show that consciousness could survive the switch, supporting substrate independence?

passages.quote: But the argument fails at its first hurdle, given the impossibility of replacing any part of the brain with a perfect silicon equivalent.

questions.question: Doesn't Bostrom's simulation argument quietly rely on the very assumption about computers and consciousness that the essay disputes?

passages.quote: This, perhaps unsurprisingly, is the assumption that “a computer running a suitable program would be conscious” (see page 2 of his paper).

questions.question: The four arguments against computation being enough for consciousness are each said to stand alone—so how do they actually reinforce each other?

passages.quote: But taken together, they complement and strengthen each other. Questioning computational functionalism reinforces the importance of distinguishing simulation from instantiation.

questions.question: If it's genuinely uncertain whether AI could be conscious, why does the author still insist we shouldn't try to create it?

passages.quote: All theories of consciousness are fraught with uncertainty, and anyone who claims to know for sure what it would take to create real artificial consciousness, or for sure what it would take to avoid doing so, is overstepping what can reasonably be said.
nobody should be deliberately setting out to create conscious AI, whether in the service of some poorly thought-through techno-rapture, or for any other reason.

questions.question: If digital computers likely can't be conscious, could some other technology accidentally create machine consciousness instead?

passages.quote: For my money, we ought to be more worried about the accidental emergence of consciousness in cerebral organoids (brain-like structures typically grown from human embryonic stem cells) than in any new wave of LLM.

questions.question: If an AI merely seems conscious but isn't, why would that still matter ethically?

passages.quote: While there is inevitable uncertainty about the former, conscious-seeming systems are much, much closer.
For example, we might give AI systems “rights” that they don’t actually need, since they would not actually be conscious, restricting our ability to control them for no good reason.

questions.question: Given our history of wrongly denying moral status to animals and other humans, doesn't withholding it from AI risk repeating that mistake?

passages.quote: It is reasonable to wonder whether withholding attributions of consciousness to AI may leave us once again on the wrong side of history.
But there are good reasons why the situation with AI is likely to be different.
